title: Chapter 1. The Toolbox for a Data Scientist: R Markdown, git, GitHub, R, and RStudio
text:
To be a data scientist, you don’t just need to know math; you need to know how to use the “tools of the trade.” This chapter introduces the ecosystem we will use to ensure our work is reproducible and professional.






TipWhy this matters for MAT 186



According to our course outline (ECO), mastering git and GitHub is not just about storage—it is about Reproducibility, a core pillar of modern data science.




Before we install the software, let’s look at the path data takes from a raw file to a finished report.






NoteAccessibility: Workflow Breakdown




Import: Loading data into R from various sources.
Tidy: Organizing data so each variable is a column and each observation is a row.
The Loop: We repeatedly Transform, Visualize, and Model data to find patterns.
Communicate: Sharing your findings using R Markdown/Quarto and GitHub.







In Lab 1: R and RStudio Installation, you will set up your environment: * R: The programming language that processes data. * RStudio: The Integrated Development Environment (IDE) where you write scripts and view results.




In Lab 2: RStudio Project and Quarto Documents, we introduce literate programming. This allows us to combine narrative text, mathematical notation (LaTeX), and executable code in one reproducible document.




In Lab 4: GitHub Repository, you will connect your local computer to the cloud. git tracks your changes, while GitHub hosts your professional portfolio. This ensures your work meets the highest standards of scientific reproducibility.




Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. (2023). R for Data Science (2e).

title: MAT 186: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Course Goals
Upon successfully completing this course, students will be able to

Perform exploratory data analysis on both univariate and bivariate data, including construction of appropriate graphical representations of the data, written descriptions of the distributions, as well as the choice and presentation of appropriate summary measures of center and spread.
Perform a correlation and regression analysis of bivariate and multivariate data, including choice of appropriate data transformations, analysis of model, and interpretation of results.
Construct and interpret both parametric and nonparametric confidence intervals concerning population means, population proportions, and independence of two binary categorical variables, and communicate results in clear written format.
Perform both parametric and nonparametric hypothesis tests concerning population means, population proportions, and independence of two binary categorical variables, and interpret and communicate results in clear written format.
Make use of the statistical software R to accomplish the above outcomes.
Critique data collection techniques, as well as basic design of experiments.
Master the Data Science workflow (Import, Tidy, Transform, Visualize, Model, Communicate).
Build reproducible reports using Quarto and GitHub.

title: Chapter 2. Introduction to R programming
text:
2.2 Accessing R Packages
Packages are collections of functions, documentation, and sample data sets written by the R community to solve specific problems. In MAT 186, we use the tidyverse package as our primary toolkit.
To use a package, you must follow a two-step process:

Installation: This downloads the package from CRAN (the R “App Store”) to your hard drive. You typically only need to do this once per computer.
Accessing (Loading): This “opens the app” and loads the functions into your current R session. You must do this every time you restart RStudio.


The Analogy: The Smartphone








Step
R Command
Smartphone Equivalent




Step 1
install.packages("tidyverse")
Downloading an App from the App Store.


Step 2
library(tidyverse)
Tapping the App icon to open it.









ImportantSyntax Reminder



Note that when you install, the package name must be in quotes: "tidyverse". When you load the library, quotes are not required.




Code
# Do this once
# install.packages("tidyverse")

# Do this at the start of every script
library(tidyverse)

2.3 Reading Data into R
In Lab 5, we move beyond simple vectors and import full datasets. Data scientists rarely type in their own data; they read it from external files. The most common format is the CSV (Comma Separated Values) file.

Loading the Low Birth Weight (LBW) Dataset
For our analysis, we will use the lbw.csv dataset, which contains information on risk factors associated with low birth weight.
To read this file into R, we use the read_csv() function from the tidyverse library:

title: Chapter 2. Introduction to R programming
text:
2.4 Writing R Functions
If you need to perform the same task multiple times, you should write a function. Functions encapsulate a sequence of operations into a single command, making your code more readable and less prone to error.
A function consists of: 1. A Name: What you call the function (e.g., grams_to_lbs). 2. Arguments: The input data the function needs to work. 3. The Body: The code inside the curly braces {} that performs the math.

Example: Converting Birth Weight
The lbw.csv dataset records birth weight in grams (bwt). We can write a function to convert those values to pounds.


Code
# Defining the function
grams_to_lbs <- function(grams) {
  lbs <- grams * 0.00220462
  return(lbs)
}

# Testing the function with a single value
grams_to_lbs(3000)


[1] 6.61386


Code
# Applying the function to the 'bwt' column in our dataset
lbw_data$bwt_lbs <- grams_to_lbs(lbw_data$bwt)

title: Chapter 2. Introduction to R programming
section: 2.5 Organizing and Commenting on R Code
text:
2.5 Organizing and Commenting on R Code
According to our ECO, code must be well-documented and organized to ensure Reproducibility. A reproducible script is one that a peer (or your future self) can run and understand without needing to ask you questions.

Best Practices for MAT 186

1. The “Why” Rule of Commenting
Use the # symbol to write comments. Comments should explain the logic or justification for a step, not just describe the code.

Weak: library(tidyverse) # load tidyverse (The code already says this).
Strong: library(tidyverse) # loading toolkit for data import and wrangling



2. Code Sections
Use RStudio’s section headers (Ctrl + Shift + R) to create a table of contents for your script. This makes long analyses of datasets like lbw.csv much easier to navigate.


3. Consistent Naming
Always use snake_case (all lowercase with underscores) for your objects. * Good: lbw_clean, low_birth_weight_analysis * Avoid: LBWData, Data1, test



Example of an Organized Script
Here is how your script for Lab 5 should look:


Code
# --- 1. Setup & Data Import ---
# Purpose: Analyze risk factors for low birth weight
library(tidyverse)
lbw <- read_csv("data/lbw.csv")


Rows: 189 Columns: 11
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

lbw$bwt_lbs <- grams_to_lbs(lbw$bwt)

title: Chapter 3. Getting and Wrangling Data
text:
NoteLearning Objectives (ECO Alignment)



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Explain the difference between raw and tidy data. 2. Utilize codebooks to interpret data variables. 3. Clean data using dplyr verbs (filter, select, mutate). 4. Handle missing values and rename variables for clarity.



3.1 Raw Data vs. Tidy Data
Data rarely arrives in a format ready for analysis. Raw data is often “messy”—it may have inconsistent formatting, missing values, or confusing headers.
In this course, we aim for Tidy Data: 1. Each variable forms a column. 2. Each observation forms a row. 3. Each type of observational unit forms a table.


3.2 Codebooks and Data Collection
Before cleaning data, you must understand it. A Codebook (or data dictionary) is a document that describes the contents, structure, and layout of a dataset.
For the lbw.csv dataset, the codebook tells us: * low: Indicator of birth weight less than 2.5kg (0 = No, 1 = Yes). * smoke: Smoking status during pregnancy (0 = No, 1 = Yes). * lwt: Mother’s weight in pounds at the last menstrual period.


3.3 Data Manipulation with dplyr
In Lab 7, we use the dplyr package (part of the Tidyverse) to manipulate our data. We use the pipe operator %>% (or |>) to chain functions together.

Key “Verbs” for Data Cleaning:

select(): Pick specific columns (e.g., only age and bwt).
filter(): Pick rows based on conditions (e.g., only mothers who smoke).
mutate(): Create new columns (like we did with grams_to_lbs).
rename(): Change column names to be more descriptive.



Code
library(tidyverse)

3.4 Handling Missing Data and Outliers
Real-world data often has missing values, represented as NA in R.
When cleaning data, we must decide:
Remove: Delete rows with missing values using drop_na().
Impute: Replace missing values with a mean or median.
Identify Outliers: Use logical filters to find values that are physically impossible (e.g., a birth weight of 0 grams).

title: MAT 186: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Official Course Description
This course introduces the basic ideas and techniques of data science including: exploratory data analysis; experimental design and sampling; relationships between one and several variables including single and multiple regression and two-way tables; sampling distributions; inferential statistics for means, proportions, and regression coefficients; and simple ANOVA.
The course includes a significant computer component using the software package R.
Prerequisite: Placement level 4 (see DCC Math Placement Table) or MAT 184 with a grade of C or better.

text:
The Computer Component
As an OER-driven course, we prioritize open-source tools. You will develop a professional portfolio using: * R & RStudio: For data processing and statistical analysis. * Quarto: For creating reproducible, high-quality technical reports. * GitHub: For version control and sharing your work with the global community.

section: Key Aspects of MAT 186 and the Program
text:
Key Aspects of MAT 186 and the Program

Career Readiness & Microcredentials
MAT 186 is a core component of our three-course Data Analysis microcredential. This program is specifically designed to prepare students for careers as junior data analysts, focusing on practical applications for business and marketing analytics.

Course Focus: We cover data visualization, data cleaning, and statistical analysis to interpret complex data patterns.
Technical Skills: Students master industry-standard tools and programming languages, specifically R, RStudio, and Quarto.



Institutional Distinction
Dutchess Community College (DCC) is proud to be the first community college in the nation with an American Statistical Association (ASA) Student Chapter. This connection provides our students with unique networking and professional development opportunities in the field of statistics.

title: Chapter 4. Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
NoteLearning Objectives (ECO Alignment)



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. Apply the “Grammar of Graphics” to create professional visualizations. 2. Perform Univariate Analysis to understand the distribution of a single variable. 3. Perform Multivariate Analysis to identify relationships between two or more variables. 4. Interpret patterns, outliers, and clusters in real-world data like lbw.csv.



4.1 The Philosophy of EDA
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is an iterative cycle. We use visualization and transformation to explore our data, looking for patterns or anomalies before we move on to formal statistical modeling.


4.2 Principles of Data Graphics: ggplot2
In R, we use the ggplot2 package, which is based on the Grammar of Graphics. Every plot is built in layers: 1. Data: The dataframe (e.g., lbw). 2. Aesthetics (aes): The mapping of variables to visual properties (x-axis, y-axis, color). 3. Geoms: The geometric shapes (bars, points, lines).


4.3 Univariate Analysis
We begin by looking at one variable at a time. This helps us understand the “shape” of our data (skewness, central tendency, and spread).

Numerical Variables: Histograms
```r library(tidyverse) lbw <- read_csv(“data/lbw.csv”)



Visualizing the distribution of mother’s weight (lwt)
ggplot(lbw, aes(x = lwt)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = “steelblue”, color = “white”) + labs(title = “Distribution of Maternal Weight”, x = “Weight (lbs)”, y = “Count”)
